<question>
Can a tenant alter or decorate the rented home without the landlord's permission? Compare Spain, Colombia and Dubai.
</question>

<answer>
Spain: a tenant may not carry out works that change the configuration of the dwelling or its accessories without the landlord's written consent [1]. Tenants may never carry out works that reduce the stability or safety of the dwelling [1]. If the landlord did not authorise the works, he may require the tenant to restore the previous state at the end of the contract, or he may keep the change without paying compensation [1]. Colombia: improvements, changes or extensions made without the landlord's express authorisation are a ground on which the landlord may ask to end the contract [2]. Dubai: a tenant may not make changes or carry out restoration or maintenance works unless the landlord permits them and the required licences have been obtained [3]. For decoration works that need official approvals and do not affect the structure, the landlord must provide the approvals [4].
</answer>

<reference>
Spain: the tenant may not, without the landlord's written consent, carry out works that change the configuration of the dwelling or its accessories, and may never carry out works that reduce its stability or safety; if the landlord did not authorise them, he may require the tenant to restore the previous state at the end of the contract, or keep the change without paying compensation (art. 23 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). Colombia: improvements, changes or extensions made without the landlord's express authorisation are a ground on which the landlord may ask to end the contract (art. 22, point 5, of Ley 820 de 2003). Dubai: the tenant may not make changes or carry out restoration or maintenance works unless the landlord permits them and after obtaining the required licences (art. 19 of Law No. (26) of 2007); for decoration works that need official approvals and do not affect the structure, the landlord must provide the approvals (art. 18).
</reference>

Extra correct detail is fine. Leaving out a condition or exception that the reference treats as essential fails, and so does any statement that contradicts the reference. Wording, order and length do not matter. If the reference says part of the question cannot be answered from the law, the answer must leave that part open too, not fill it in.

In your reasoning, name the rule the reference states, then say whether the answer states it, leaves part of it out, or contradicts it.

The answer states each of these rules with the same content and conditions: Spain's written consent, stability prohibition, restoration or keep-without-compensation options; Colombia's ground for termination on unauthorised changes; Dubai's permission and licence requirement and the landlord's duty to provide approvals for decoration not affecting structure.
